column2: Act Four
Dance of the Flame Demon Blade
Sword Devil with Flaming Rage

Chu Zihang paused briefly and looked around, holding the sword across his left arm, its point sloping down as ink-dark drops fell slowly from it. More black shapes stepped out of the mist. He had no time to distinguish reality from illusion, just as on that night in the typhoon. Then he had been a frail boy; now he had set his dragon blood alight. Without hesitation, without asking why, he sent a storm of blades cutting through the fog once more.
What were his enemies? He needed only to cut them down!
Cassell College headquarters, central control room.

“Our opponents are hunters. Some may have dragon blood. Since this recovery operation is on Chinese soil and we don't want trouble with the police, we need to strike fast and finish quickly, so we're deploying a nine-person team. The Board of Trustees has approved the plan. We'll direct it remotely from here.” Manstein glanced at his watch. “Forty-five minutes until the operation begins.”
A three-dimensional model of the Runde Building hung projected in the air. Schneider walked slowly around it.
“Where's Mingfei?” Guderian flipped through the plan. “I don't see what Mingfei is responsible for.”
“Coordinating command. A very important job,” Manstein said. He had left Lu Mingfei out of the plan because his coursework showed so little training that he was incapable of taking on any assignment.
Guderian nodded in understanding.

“Our central objective is the twenty-first floor of Tower A, the headquarters of Millennium. The documents should be there,” Manstein said. “The Runde Building has twin towers. The company owns the entire twenty-first floor of Tower A.”
“It's only an office building. Isn't a nine-person team a little extravagant?” Guderian said. “You look as if you're planning to take the Pentagon!”

“If we were taking the Pentagon, we'd need seven more people,” Schneider said expressionlessly. “Security at the Runde Building is tight. The developer contracted it out to these hunters, so their people are all over the building. They know their business can't stand public scrutiny, so this is how they protect themselves.” He waved, and the model changed to a cross section. Every route was marked in red: stairs, elevators, fire escapes, even ventilation ducts. “Security controls every route. To reach Tang Wei on the twenty-first floor by elevator, you have to transfer once and pass four checkpoints. Worst of all, the bottom five floors are retail, and the crowds will slow us down. If the operation takes more than five minutes, the police will arrive, and the hunters will have time to move the documents.”
“Five minutes?” Guderian asked, puzzled. “The elevator might not even get there in five minutes.”
“We aren't taking the elevator,” Manstein said. “We're taking a direct route!”

At 18:15, as the sun sank westward, Chu Zihang looked up at the building's glass curtain wall, where advancing clouds of dusk were reflected. Static crackled in his earpiece as campus headquarters reconnected with him across the Pacific.
“Have you read the operation plan?” Schneider's hoarse voice came through the earpiece.

“It's a low-difficulty operation. If the opposition has no one with a high concentration of dragon blood, I can do it alone. I don't need that support,” Chu Zihang said. “The Maintenance Department people are too conspicuous.”

“Obey orders,” Schneider said. “We've told them to wear civilian clothes and keep a low profile. They'll meet you in thirty minutes. Another team has, as you requested...” Schneider paused. “Gone to Lu Mingfei's home.”
“Understood.”

“This is China. Don't mistake it for an unpoliced stretch of the West African desert and make too much noise!” Schneider lowered his voice. “There are problems in your past record. You know that yourself. Don't draw the college's scrutiny.”
“Understood,” Chu Zihang said. “But you are the college, Professor.”

Schneider was momentarily at a loss. “All right! That's enough! This is a discreet operation: no helmets, guns, blades, tactical flashlights, and certainly none of the alchemical equipment supplied by those lunatics in the Equipment Department. To the police it shouldn't look like an organized break-in...”
“But a bank robbery,” Chu Zihang said suddenly.
Schneider blinked. “Yes... it does look a little like one...”

At 18:30, Tang Wei was playing Plants vs. Zombies while waiting for the courier who was to collect the package. His nagging father was waiting for him to come home for dinner, and he was getting anxious. Tang Wei had once been a street thug, the sort of bully who would lift the skirts of girls passing him in summer just to look. But when his father got angry and came after him waving a spatula, he never dared fight back; he covered his head and ran. His underlings asked, Boss, what are you scared of? You're so tough, and you're a head and a half taller than your dad. Tang Wei smacked one of them on the forehead. “A dad's valuable because he's rare! You only get one. Break him and there's no replacement!”
Tang Wei picked up the phone. “Front desk? Has anyone come to collect the package?”
“No, Mr. Tang. It looks like rain. I doubt they'll come today,” the receptionist said in a beguiling voice.
“It was sunny all afternoon. How can it suddenly be raining?” Tang Wei looked out the window. Clouds were slowly pressing over the city, black with the promise of a storm.
The sudden change in weather made him uneasy, as though something were about to happen. He logged in to the Hunter Market for one last look.

He entered his ID, “3rd_young_master,” and password. When he pressed Enter, the page refreshed from top to bottom: black background, dark green lines, deep red type, like a door opening before him onto another world. Bored, he clicked through the sections, reviewed his mission history, and considered posting a farewell in the chat area. His friends would probably send messages wishing the Third Young Master well in a lovely land full of beautiful legs and so on. So touching.
A notice flashed at the upper right: “You have one unread message.”
The message contained a single word: “Byebye.”
Someone had guessed he was retiring? Who was clever enough to read his mind? Tang Wei looked at the sender field... It was blank.
There was no sender.

At that instant, thunder shook the windows. They flashed deathly white as a vertical bolt illuminated the Runde Building. Tens of thousands of volts of static electricity made every lit window flicker. At last the rain came down.

Tang Wei began to tremble. He had the worst feeling imaginable: the message came from his client on this job, that very manly Ronald McDonald. And “Byebye” wasn't wishing him a pleasant boat ride down a Vietnamese river, admiring beauties.
The word could also mean farewell forever.

At 18:40, a black BMW glided along a quiet, tree-lined road. Rain poured down. Looking out the window, Lu Mingfei saw an old red-brick house by the lake, appearing and disappearing in the curtain of rain at the end of the road.

The old mansion was called Number One Lake Garden because it was the only numbered address on the entire road. Its heavy black wrought-iron gates stood open. The car drove straight through and stopped before the house.

The house was completely dark. Through the huge floor-to-ceiling windows he could see empty tables covered in checked cloths, but no one inside. The door was closed, and the only light burned above it. A waiter in white stood in the rain beneath an umbrella.
“Come on, they got it wrong, didn't they? The place is closed,” Lu Mingfei muttered to himself. The driver had already opened his door.
“Aspasia has been reserved for a private party tonight, sir,” the waiter said politely.

“Oh, great!” Already nervous and awkward, Lu Mingfei felt reprieved and turned to escape. But the waiter slowly pushed open the locked door. “Mr. Ricardo M. Lu, you are our only honored guest tonight.”
Lu Mingfei's head buzzed. Only then did he realize the club leaders had even more clout than he had imagined: they had reserved the whole of Aspasia for him!

Soft music began. The waiter in white walked into the dark center of the old house and struck a match to light the floating candles on the table. In the warm glow sat Chen Wenwen, dressed in white, a white butterfly clip in her black hair.
Time seemed to race backward. Lu Mingfei returned to the afternoon four years ago when they had first met.

At 18:45, on the street outside the Runde Building, people ran in every direction through the downpour, holding all sorts of things over their heads, and the street suddenly emptied. Chu Zihang stood beneath an umbrella in the gloom, holding a long box marked “Flower Delivery.” Head bowed, he watched huge drops strike the ground and shatter into transparent flowers.

A van marked “FedEx” pierced the curtain of rain and stopped in front of him with a shriek of brakes. The formidable support team headquarters had assigned to him jumped out one after another, moving as if cast from the same mold. Clearly they were well-trained elites.
“Civilian clothes and a low profile, just as promised. Refreshing,” Chu Zihang remarked mildly.

The brawny maintenance men stood shoulder to shoulder as if awaiting inspection, though their clothes were somewhat unconventional. One wore an Adiwang pullover, another wide-legged Korean-style pants, and another oversized Double Star skate shoes. Their leader wore the green uniform of Beijing Guoan, apparently a devoted fan.
“Not appropriate?” The leader looked himself over. “I thought this was how Chinese people dressed.”
“But our chest muscles don't look as if they're about to burst out of our shirts.” Chu Zihang surveyed their bodybuilding-champion physiques.
“We can't exactly hide our muscles in our pockets...” The leader looked troubled.

“Never mind. It won't affect anything, except that tomorrow you'll make the evening paper's front page: ‘Adiwang's American Muscle Men Brazenly Rob Office Building.’ You should have read the plan. You have five minutes to prepare. Professor Schneider will send orders directly to your earpieces.” Chu Zihang waved, carried the box toward the Runde Building, and smiled at the guards. “Hello. Courier service. Flower delivery.”
At 18:50, Chu Zihang was in the high-speed elevator to the top floor, the numbers flying past.
At 18:52, Lu Mingfei gazed into Chen Wenwen's eyes across the candlelight as the waiter poured them rose-colored aperitifs.
At 18:53, Tang Wei hurriedly packed up his office. He didn't want to wait anymore. He could leave the delivery to an underling. On this damned rainy day, he wanted to get home early.
At 18:54, guards on every floor of the Runde Building received a call: post extra personnel in the rain and make sure the building was secure. All surveillance systems were switched on.
Manstein looked down at his carefully synchronized watch, headset on, all channels to China open. The second hand ticked forward.
At 18:55 Beijing time, Manstein said, “Operation commence,” and started the stopwatch on his watch.

He knew the order would set a precision machine in motion: the nine-person team at the Runde Building. Each was a gear with a different function, yet each worked with the others. Every plan was different, every assignment decided in advance. If they followed the procedure, they would have the objective in five minutes.

The man in the Adiwang sportswear crossed the rain toward the building's front entrance. His very “localized” civilian clothes did nothing to hide the aggression of those enormous muscles. The guards stepped back and reached for their batons. Wherever these men went, they looked like a gang of thugs.

Adiwang spread his arms, blocking the guards' blows with his hard forearms, then grabbed two by the collars and hoisted them into the air. Alarms rang, startling the entire shopping area. Customers sheltering from the rain and doing a little shopping had packed the ground floor; now they all looked toward the entrance. Adiwang was already tangled up with a dozen guards. He sprinted between the luxury shops on the first floor, nothing able to obstruct him. A burst of speed carried him over a five-foot display sign like a hurdler. The stunned guards could only weave around the crowd. Whenever he found he'd left them too far behind, he stopped, looked back, and gave them an idiotic grin.
The shoppers were baffled. Had a bodybuilding coach gone crazy? Was this a parkour show put on to entertain customers? Whatever it was, watching the fools chase one another was rather fun.

But soon they sensed something was wrong. Guards poured out of different exits and raced down the escalators. A burly man in a pullover and Double Star shoes ran up an escalator moving downward, taking several steps at a stride. Like a cannonball, he struck the guards and pinned them in the middle. The escalator went down, but the people stayed where they were.

The man in the green Beijing Guoan jersey took the emergency stairs to the second floor, kicked in the surveillance-room door, and shattered the control panel with one punch. He pulled out two wires and touched them together; the excess current burned the equipment out completely.
A professional robbery gang could hardly have done better.
“Everybody down! Hands on your heads!” Adiwang roared in less than perfect Chinese.

He had plunged into the crowd, with guards converging from every direction. He didn't want to fight them; in hand-to-hand combat, one shoulder throw would break their backs. The words came out instinctively. When he had served in the SEALs on counterterrorism missions, he had always shouted that at hostages before emptying his submachine gun into the terrorists.
The customers screamed, crouched, and put their hands on their heads.

“They're awfully cooperative, aren't they?” Adiwang was pleased by the Chinese public's counterterrorism awareness. On past missions in Europe, he had often encountered hostages whose legs went weak and who shook too hard to cooperate.
His satisfaction lasted only a second. He suddenly saw the pretty girl in front of him crouch and hold up the wallet she had taken from her bag as though presenting a treasure.
Damn it! They really thought it was a robbery!

The retail floors were in chaos. All the guards converged there, scattered in every direction by the huge men acting like a pack of fools. The ropes holding a wall of balloons on the first floor were untied, and the balloons rose slowly. From the second floor someone poured down paper-cut dandelions meant for the Qixi celebration, filling the air with little spinning parachutes. Someone hurled handfuls of glow sticks from a nearby display into the crowd. A giant ball of flowers was pulled from the center of the dome and burst in the air, thousands of silk flowers floating like a sea of blossoms.

The Maintenance Department elites were having a good time. This was a simple assignment: draw the guards into the shops and blind the surveillance system, leaving the rest to the man among them with the strongest bloodline. They only had to play with the guards for five minutes.
They didn't notice the van they had left in the rain shudder to life and roll slowly toward the front entrance. Its wipers were off, and rain on the windshield hid the driver.

On the roof, Chu Zihang stood in the pouring rain, holding the “Flower Delivery” box. The Runde Building was forty-six stories and 210 meters tall. Looking down from the edge of the roof, everything seemed so small that he felt far removed from the whole world.
Lonely. Vast and open.
Chu Zihang let his body tip forward and plunged straight down!
In complete weightlessness, he drew the sword from the box. Shreds of flowers flew, and the sacred sword Murasame shrieked as it cut the air.

On the twenty-first floor of Tower A, guards had blocked every entrance, from the stairwells to the elevators. At Tang Wei's order, they had all mobilized. Millennium was nominally a security company, and they were professionals: its eighty or ninety men were no pushovers. The building had called the police, so even armed opponents shouldn't necessarily have been able to fight their way up. The guards couldn't understand why Tang Wei was so nervous. Besides, the banks were all downstairs; on this floor there was only their security company, full of big men and the smell of sweat and cigarettes. Bank robbers shouldn't make it their first stop.
“Hey, hey! Someone's jumping!” one guard said, pointing out the window.

Most saw a figure flash downward. Then came the sharp twang of a steel cable tightening and the creak of turning gears. An enormous dark shape rose outside the window. A courier in sunglasses stood in the rain, carrying a long sheathed sword. He unfastened the rappelling clip at his waist and threw the bare flower stems into the wind.

This was his direct route. He had fallen wearing a rappelling clip, while the Maintenance Department had activated the suspended platform used to wash the glass curtain wall. As the platform rose and Chu Zihang descended, he used the clip to slow himself and landed safely.

It looked elaborate, but was actually simple and practical: the optimal route Norma had devised after analyzing the entire building. The disturbance in the shops concealed the purpose of the operation, allowed control of the platform, and kept the mass of guards downstairs occupied.

Four minutes and forty seconds remained. Chu Zihang only had to clear the floor and retrieve the documents within that time. In the underground garage, the Panamera was already running, a maintenance man at the wheel. The garage entrance had been blocked, causing traffic to jam on the western road in a sea of red lights. The eastern road had been cleared. Once Chu Zihang reached the ground, he could leave immediately by car.
The timing was entirely under control. The plan was flawless, every piece meshing with the next.
The guards stared as the courier pressed a device resembling a stun gun against the tempered glass. Current flashed, the whole pane began to vibrate at high frequency, and then it shattered.

Chu Zihang entered the twenty-first floor. The guards had no time to think; they drew their electric batons and surrounded him. The two in front stepped forward together and struck at his head. By the standards of a martial-arts school, they were excellent students, each capable of fighting three or five men. But that was against people, and their opponent now... could hardly be called truly “human.”

Chu Zihang suddenly accelerated. Before the raised batons could fall, he was chest to chest with the two guards. He pressed his hands against their chests, paused an instant, and released his power. He had chosen tai chi as his martial-arts elective; its soft, yielding force sent two men weighing over 150 jin reeling into the walls on either side. He caught the next two by the neck and spun seemingly lightly. The rotation flung them away, each knocking down two more guards. The others were stunned. There had been ten of them; six were down in an instant, and their opponent had clearly not even begun to fight in earnest. His sword was still in its sheath.

An entire squad of guards crowded into the corridor. Their comrades, unaware of what had happened, had come as reinforcements, full of energy. What kind of petty thief was this? Robbing a bank branch and frightening pretty girls was one thing, but invading a security company was asking for death.

Chu Zihang frowned slightly. This squad would cost him more time. Then he heard a distant chant, like the chanting of ancient monks. A domain unfolded without a sound. The skin of every guard present flushed red as though blood were seeping through it. Their hearts pounded, sending blood surging through their bodies, and in an instant their physical abilities multiplied. They didn't even notice the change, but threw themselves at Chu Zihang with all their strength.

Yanling: King's Attendants, sequence number twenty-eight. It strengthened the bodies of living creatures within its domain. In ancient times, dragons had used it to inspire the humans and even beasts loyal to them, strengthening them into an army.

The intelligence had been slightly off. Norma had not mentioned a hybrid like this in the security company. Twenty-eight was not a high sequence number, but this Yanling strengthened companions, and a whole floor of companions surrounded its user.
Hidden from everyone's view in the shadows at the far end of the corridor, a slender figure chanted softly, faint gold flowing in their eyes.

The storm raged behind him; crowds of guards filled the passage ahead. Trapped in the narrow space, Chu Zihang did not retreat. Surging forward, the guards leaped, driven by a dose of adrenaline that had instantly doubled in their bloodstreams. High-voltage batons crisscrossed the air, static breaking through it in fine purple filaments that linked one baton to another.
Their display was intimidating, but still not enough to threaten Chu Zihang. There was a fundamental difference between hybrids and ordinary humans, however much the latter were strengthened.

Chu Zihang sprang back to avoid the blows. He leaped through the floor-to-ceiling window into the storm, where one last foothold remained: the suspended platform. It bought him a few brief seconds to find a reasonable answer to this surprise. Against physically enhanced opponents, he would have to strike harder, but that would inevitably injure them, and when the enhancement faded, the injuries would remain in full.

Chu Zihang rubbed his fingers together. They were unusually damp. He had overlooked something strange: the humidity on the twenty-first floor was extraordinarily high. More precisely, the air was oversaturated with moisture, faintly white like thick fog. The dense vapor had turned the air into a conductor, allowing the batons to spark between one another. But even during a storm, the humidity inside a centrally air-conditioned building should not have been so high.
The guards did not pursue him. Instead, they stopped together and formed a human wall in front of him. For an instant their faces all looked identical.
Chu Zihang shivered. The scene felt familiar: surrounded by a crowd of identical, expressionless faces.
Then he caught a familiar scent: the scent of a cold rainstorm, unique, one he had smelled only once before, on that elevated road shrouded in sheets of water!
A car horn sounded below. Chu Zihang looked down. On the deserted street to the east, a rust-spotted Maybach, headlights on, was driving slowly toward Tower A of the Runde Building.

Terror exploded in his heart. The Maybach's engine roared as it drove straight into a load-bearing pillar on the side of the building. Its heavy body struck at over a hundred miles an hour; the pillar tore its front end in two, and the entire building shook. The suspended platform jolted. Its cables slipped off the gears, caught between the bearings, and were twisted apart. Chu Zihang lost his balance as the entire platform fell!
He understood at once why the guards hadn't pursued him. They had merely wanted to force him into a death trap. They had succeeded.
Portofino, Italy.
Amid whirling leaves, a silver Rolls-Royce climbed the winding mountain road into the Splendid Hotel and stopped beside a white building close to the cliff.

The detached building had walls of hard white marble and narrow little windows, like a tiny fortress. Its private parking lot was nearly full: a Lamborghini, a vintage Jaguar, an AMG-modified Mercedes. Surprisingly, an orange mountain bike occupied an entire space alongside the luxury cars.

The driver bent to open the door, shielding its upper edge with his hand so the honored guest wouldn't bump her head. A golden high heel touched the ground, followed by a slender, breathtakingly beautiful leg. Unlike the aristocratic lady the shoe suggested, the passenger was a young woman with features as exquisite as a sculpture by a Greek master. She looked twenty, but her eyes belonged to someone in her thirties. She wore the makeup of a European grande dame, a black veil, an expensive fitted skirt suit, and a fur stole. Her slender heels gave her a swaying grace as she walked, but her cold face carried the imperious air of a queen.

“The sixth trustee, and the last. Elizabeth Laurent, twenty-two. Her family owns one of Europe's largest syndicates, with interests in mining and finance. After her father died in a plane crash, she had to interrupt her studies at the Royal Academy of Arts to inherit the business.” Not far from the white building, behind the blinds of a hotel suite, a secretary named Parsi explained patiently.
“A woman who thinks she's very beautiful.” Caesar lifted a slat and peered out.
“Indeed. Her family was once famous among hybrids for producing beautiful descendants.” Parsi smiled.
“Hello, Liza, my child! Welcome, welcome. Right on time.” An old man strode out to meet her, arms open. “You've grown again. I still remember you in your Eton uniform.”
“Thank you, Anjou.” She embraced him and exchanged cheek kisses. “You haven't seen me in eight years, then. You look just the same. Time seems to have stopped for you.”
“For an old man, the god of time takes pity and lets the clock run a little more slowly.” The old man offered her his arm like a gentleman.
She took it and climbed the stairs with him, like a beautiful daughter entering society for the first time with her elderly but still handsome father.
Principal Anjou of Cassell College.
“There should be one more trustee,” Caesar said.
“I've never seen him attend, and I don't know his name,” Parsi said.
“He spends enormous sums on the college every year but never comes to exercise the power he's entitled to. Magnificent.”
“The trustees don't invest in Cassell College for money. They are,” Parsi said softly, “the secret party of dragon-slaying families!”

A secret organization that had endured for thousands of years, an elite legion of hybrids that had trained countless brave fighters under an iron code—the Dragon Blood Secret Party had, in the modern world, taken the form of a college board of trustees.
“They're also this generation's council of elders, aren't they?” Caesar asked.
“Yes. The board and the council of elders are one and the same. The trustees are the highest class among hybrids, the true holders of power. Principal Anjou is only the executive they chose.”
“All I can do is wait here until they call me in?” Caesar sipped the strong liquor in his glass.

“They're looking forward to meeting you. They'll certainly summon you.” Parsi bowed slightly. “That's why your uncle arranged this year's annual board meeting at the Splendid: so you could make your formal appearance somewhere familiar and meet the people who hold power among hybrids.”
“People who hold power?” Caesar savored the words.
The building's doors slowly closed from within. Four heavy ancient locks clicked shut together, sealing it completely.
“Everyone is here, so I declare this year's annual board meeting open.” Seated at the end of the long table, Anjou shook a small brass bell.

The place had once been used by ancient monks for austere religious practice, so it was unusually dark. Though it was daytime, a row of candlesticks stood on the table, illuminating the trustees' faces.

There were six in all, four men and two women. On either side of Anjou sat two men so old their ages could no longer be guessed. Both wore crisp black suits with dark red handkerchiefs in their breast pockets. One leaned on a cane; the other fingered a string of rosewood beads and muttered under his breath, looking somewhat out of place. Another man, perhaps in his thirties or forties, wore a bright yellow tracksuit, with a bicycle helmet beside his right hand. A trustee of an elite school like Cassell College had actually ridden a bicycle to the meeting. The trustee beside Liza was startlingly young, a girl of sixteen or seventeen. Her long pale-gold hair was piled on her head, and her still baby-fat face was serious as an exquisite doll's. A butler in white gloves stood erect behind her, head high and chest out.

“The same people are here as last year. The one who never attends is absent as usual, and the Gattuso family has again sent Frost Gattuso, my old friend, in his brother's place.” Anjou indicated the old man with the cane beside him.

Frost Gattuso picked up the bell in front of him and rang it. “Is the Bronze Report ready? I'm eager to know the conclusion.” Ringing before speaking was a board tradition meant to prevent interruptions.
“It's the stack of papers in front of each of you,” Anjou said.
As one, the trustees flipped through the elaborate report to the last page. The conclusion read: “The Monarch of Fire & Bronze was terminated.”
Though the college taught Chinese, the report was in English for the trustees from different language backgrounds. It meant: the King of Bronze and Fire had been killed.

The trustees were silent for a moment before this definitive conclusion. It was an epoch-making event, and the final report had taken half a year to prepare so there would be no mistake. Though they had all anticipated the conclusion, seeing the words with their own eyes still required a moment of quiet acceptance.
Frost rang again. “No Dragon King in history has ever been confirmed dead. Anjou, you need to produce evidence.”

Without a word, Anjou took out a prismatic crystal and slid it along the table. The trustees exchanged glances. At last the old man with the beads picked it up and squinted at it against the light. It was artificial quartz, bearing the logo of an optical-products company in Texas. Its slightly convex surface acted as a magnifying glass. At its center was a dark-red line as fine as a hair, like a thread of congealed blood. The old man's pupils contracted. His hand trembled as he passed the crystal on.
“The Philosopher's Stone,” he said softly, ringing his bell. “A newly made Philosopher's Stone, indeed.”

“The crystallized ‘fifth element’ of alchemy: the Philosopher's Stone, said to turn any metal into gold, also a medicine that grants eternal life, the most sacred thing in alchemy.” Anjou nodded. “As you all know, we have lost the method of producing it. The last alchemist in history to succeed was Nicolas Flamel, at five in the evening on April 25, 1382. No one has succeeded in the six hundred years since. Our existing reserves all came from ancient tombs. But what you hold is a brand-new stone, however small. It was refined from the bones of a Dragon King. His name was Constantine.”
“Constantine is my name. I have been to the mountaintop of flames, where I melted a sea of bronze and forged the name of a god.” The girl softly recited the ancient scripture.
“Now he is dead, and the name of bronze can be written only on his gravestone.” Anjou's voice was cold and stern. “A dead god is nothing but a pile of old bones!”

After a long silence, Liza rose and applauded. The other trustees rose and joined her. Anjou stood slowly to accept their praise. Bracing both hands on the table, he looked at the candles and spoke in a low voice. “This is an epoch-making breakthrough, but before we reached this glory, tens of thousands of our comrades died along the way. I propose a moment of silence for the fallen. Their sacrifice bought us this.”
The trustees bowed their heads. The meeting room was utterly silent; faintly, waves could be heard rolling below the cliff.

When the silence ended and the trustees sat again, Frost rang his bell. “The King of Bronze and Fire produced a Philosopher's Stone only that big? And to kill him, you consumed a 2.75-gram stone ground into a bullet.”

“We used only one finger joint from the Dragon King's remains to refine it. If we destroyed all the bones, the yield would be much greater, but we aren't willing to do that yet,” Anjou said. “The stone's purpose is simply to prove that what we obtained was true dragon bone, not an empty shell. If Constantine had left an egg in a ‘burial place’ and could awaken again, we certainly couldn't have refined the stone.”
“‘A first-generation dragon cannot be killed’ was an iron rule we believed,” Liza said, ringing her bell. “Why has it now been broken?”

Anjou shrugged. “It wasn't an iron rule, only dogma. The dogma was that they were ‘immortal’; they simply had never been killed. It's really very simple. Making an egg takes time. We don't know how a Dragon King makes one for himself, but clearly it doesn't arise naturally. Kill him before he makes one, and his spirit can't transfer into it. Then he dies.”
“A Dragon King can't be unaware of that weakness,” the girl said, ringing her bell. “The first thing they do after awakening should be to make an egg.”

“Exactly. Like an alchemist who can make an elixir of immortality, each time he rises from death he should first make another dose and keep it close,” Anjou said. “But there are exceptions. First, when a Dragon King awakens, his power is incomplete at first, and he may not even have his memories. Like a hybrid, he needs time to discover his bloodline. Second, in a rage, a Dragon King will put revenge first. We used the death of the younger brother Constantine to enrage the elder, Norton. So although we haven't found Norton's bones, we have reason to believe he died too.”
“Both twins of the ‘fire’ line among the Four Monarchs were killed,” the old man with the prayer beads said thoughtfully, ringing his bell. “Are all Four Monarchs twins?”
“Possibly, but we still don't know whether twins have a special religious or genetic significance to dragons,” Anjou said.
Frost rang. “Where are Constantine's remains kept now?”
Anjou raised an eyebrow and was silent for several seconds. “Somewhere safe.”
“Somewhere you consider safe, or somewhere we all consider safe?” Frost's question seemed to lower the temperature in the room.
Anjou seemed too bored to answer. He shifted to a more comfortable position in his chair. “Only two people in the whole world can enter. It's safer than the World Bank's vault.”
“Which two?”
“One is me,” Anjou said mildly. “The other built the vault.”

“There are seven trustees, and none of us knows how to build vaults.” Frost looked straight into Anjou's eyes. “In other words, you're the only one among us who can reach the Dragon King's remains. Is that right, Principal?”
“Mm.” Anjou answered absently, taking a Havana No. 1 cigar from a cedar box. He slowly smelled it, snipped the end, warmed the body with a long match, lit it, and took a blissful puff.

Anyone could see he wanted to end the subject. The room seemed colder still. Frost Gattuso, the family representative, wore an icy expression. He was an important man who managed the whole family's business in his brother's place. His importance rested chiefly on the Gattusos' donations: they gave the college more each year than any other family, with Liza's Laurents second.

“Anjou, we greatly admire your courage and achievements in the cause of dragon slaying. But you must understand that Cassell College does not belong to you, and neither do the Dragon King's remains. You are the man we selected to manage that enterprise. In other words, you are our professional manager,” Frost said slowly.

“I think I've managed it rather well. If I'm a CEO, I've just submitted a splendid annual report: two Dragon Kings killed.” Anjou exhaled bluish smoke. “Trustee, this hardly seems the best time to question my management authority.”
Liza rang her bell. “I agree with Anjou. This is an era of outstanding achievement, and he has shown more than enough leadership.”

Frost picked up a printed document and slid it down the table to her. “Being an expert dragon slayer and being a good manager are two different things. These are the facts we've collected. Over the past ten years, the college's administrative costs have climbed steadily, with vast sums wasted in strange places. Every year, for example, Principal Anjou announces a carnival called Freedom Day, when students may do as they please on campus so long as nobody is injured. It has become an armed showdown between the college's two major clubs, consuming huge quantities of alchemical ammunition and leaving enormous repair bills every year.”

“In return the students agree to obey the rules the rest of the time and not fight with Yanling on or off campus. Youthful hormones need an outlet.” Anjou shrugged. “It's a small part of the college's enormous expenses.”
“Then your chartered flights around the world for vacations, also charged to the college, must be an even smaller part,” Frost said coldly.
Anjou scratched his graying hair. “To be honest, that costs quite a bit more than Freedom Day...”

“Principal Anjou is very popular at the college. He even has a fan club whose members call themselves Team Anjou. To them, it doesn't matter whether the board exists; with a spiritual leader like Principal Anjou, exterminating the dragons is no problem.”
“That's excessive praise.” The old fellow held his cigar between his teeth, apparently modest but positively glowing with delight.

“The Executive Department's methods have grown increasingly outrageous—or you may call them brave. They look like thugs willing to sacrifice all humanity for the great cause of dragon slaying. Our brave young people tour the world waving weapons modified by the Equipment Department like mounted Western cowboys righting wrongs. They don't hesitate to start fights in the heart of major cities. Cleaning up after them costs tens of millions of dollars every year.”
“It's all for our great cause.”

“And every year the college holds a beauty contest called Campus Star, with Principal Anjou personally judging and dancing with the beautiful young freshmen. Every evening there are parties of all kinds. Students fill basements with soap bubbles, jump in wearing swimsuits, and dance Latin dances. The campus network has such a free atmosphere... someone even dug up gossip about a department chair's first girlfriend.” Frost raised an eyebrow. “Is that also for our great cause?”

Everyone fell silent. The trustees passed the document around. It was detailed and well substantiated; under the principal's leadership, the college did indeed appear free and uninhibited... or rather, a carnival of demons.
It seemed hard to find words to defend him.
“You aren't thinking of firing me, are you?” Anjou asked leisurely.

Liza rang. “I think we can end this discussion. Compared with the great cause of dragon slaying, these are trifles! We needn't waste time on them. The board isn't a place for quarrels. Can you imagine the elders arguing over a few extra tens of thousands of gold coins a year back when we were still called the Secret Party?”

Frost rang. “We haven't said anything about firing anyone. My point is, Anjou, do your job, but don't assume the whole college should be under your control. It's time to hand the Dragon King's remains over to the board for safekeeping!”

“That's a fortune,” Anjou said, continuing to smoke. “We don't yet know what those bones, still carrying a dragon's soul, can do, but at the very least they can produce the Philosopher's Stone. What does the board intend to do with them? Or... what does the Gattuso family intend?”
Frost tapped the table. “Watch your words, Anjou. I'm speaking for the board, not the Gattuso family!”
“You can fire me as the board,” the old man said with a shrug, “but I won't hand the remains over to you. There's nothing to discuss.”

The trustees were shocked. In their experience, Anjou might be excessively unconventional at times, but he was still a model old-fashioned gentleman. Hearing such blunt defiance from the principal made them wonder whether he'd lost his mind.
The old man fingering his beads frowned and rang. “Anjou, you've exceeded your authority!”
Liza rang. “Can we stop discussing this? Custody of the dragon bones isn't on today's agenda!”

The girl glanced back at her butler and rang. “I think Principal Anjou should be reminded that the Secret Party's wealth must be entrusted to the council of elders. Only the board has the authority to dispose of the bones!”
The middle-aged man, silent until now, looked from side to side and rang. “Let's not spoil the harmony...”
Frost rang. “This is no longer a question of harmony! Exceeding his authority! That's what it is!”

The air around the table grew so heated it seemed ready to ignite. Everyone tried to speak; everyone rang a bell. The clear sounds merged into a deafening, uneasy uproar. The trustees rose as one and split into two arguing camps. Liza clearly supported Anjou; the two old men looked stern; after each glance at her butler, the girl hurled forceful words at Anjou; and the middle-aged man kept chattering, “Stay calm”...
Suddenly a more furious ringing drowned out every voice, full of impatience and ferocity.

All eyes turned to the man ringing: Anjou. The old fellow had seized several bells around him and was shaking them furiously over his head, cigar clenched between his teeth as clouds of smoke poured out. He looked rather like some villain wielding a soul-shaking bell in The Investiture of the Gods...

Anjou threw the bells onto the table, leaned back, and exhaled at length. “All right. This subject won't reach a conclusion, so we can end it. You won't fire me for now, because you can't find anyone to replace me.”

After a long silence, the trustees resumed their seats. Anjou had named the problem closest to their hearts. Supporters and opponents alike admitted that in Cassell's hundred-plus years, no one had appeared who could replace him. Behind Anjou stood the department heads, powerful supporters and elites among hybrids.
“Next item: the candidate for the Nibelungen Project.” Anjou clapped his hands. “Allow me to introduce our A-rank student, an elite beyond question: Caesar Gattuso.”

The door opened. Brilliant gold hair, sea-blue eyes, a pure-white dinner suit, and a violet silk handkerchief in his breast pocket: Caesar Gattuso appeared before the trustees in unapologetically flamboyant attire.
“So handsome!” the girl blurted out involuntarily.
The butler promptly put a hand on her shoulder. “Miss, composure.”
Embarrassed, she resumed the solemn face of a trustee, her little face stiff with the effort.
Caesar nodded slightly to everyone and sat casually in the empty seat at the end of the table.

“No student has ever been invited to a board meeting in all these years. You're the first.” Anjou glanced at Caesar, then turned to the trustees. “A brief introduction: he has just been reelected Student Council president unanimously, unprecedented in college history, though that has something to do with his turning the council into his personal fan club. His GPA is 2.7, rather poor, the same as former President George W. Bush's at Yale. Numerous tardies, two failed courses... Oh, he's one of the leaders in the armed battles on Freedom Day. He also received a warning for filling the swimming pool with beer in winter and holding a lavish beer-swimming competition, which cracked the frozen pool.”
“I wanted champagne, but buying that much of the same brand at once was a little difficult.” Caesar didn't mind the awful introduction; he merely supplemented the last point.
“The one main reason he can sit here as a candidate is that he killed the Dragon King Norton,” Anjou said.

After a moment's silence, the trustees applauded politely. This single merit erased all the preceding shortcomings. Someone who could kill a Dragon King deserved a hero's respect and a seat among the trustees.
“Unfortunately, Caesar, I can't reveal the trustees' names to you,” Anjou said. “Except one, of course: your uncle. Won't you say hello?”
Caesar seemed not to hear. From the moment he entered the room, he had not looked at Frost Gattuso, his own uncle. Nor had he ever told anyone that he belonged to a trustee's family.
“You didn't summon me here because the Gattusos sit on the board, did you?” Caesar looked at Anjou. “When I entered Cassell, I said it was my personal choice, nothing to do with the family.”
“No. It's because of a project: the Nibelungen Project,” Frost Gattuso said.
“Nibelungen?” Caesar repeated the name.

He knew it as the land of the dead in Norse mythology. In Wagner's famous opera The Ring of the Nibelung, the ring of that name represented power: whoever possessed it would possess the world. A family music teacher had taught him to appreciate opera since childhood, and he liked heroic themes.
“Before we disclose the project, we have a few questions,” Liza said. “What do you think of dragon slaying?”
“Enormous fun.” Caesar's answer was nonsensical.
The butler whispered to the girl. She nodded, fixing her dark-green, catlike eyes on Caesar. “Why slay dragons? Without following Cassell's path, you could still enjoy an aristocrat's life.”
“Isn't human existence a matter of proving oneself again and again?” His ice-blue eyes met hers without flinching. “I haven't found a better way to prove myself.”
“Good,” Anjou said. “What is your goal for the future?”
“Wait for the next Dragon King to awaken and kill him.” Caesar spread his hands. “I only hope he won't wait until I've died of old age.”
“I like that lawless tone. Frost, you see, your nephew is actually more like me than you...” Anjou smiled. “Caesar, you faced Norton directly. Did you feel his overwhelming power?”
Caesar grew grave. After a pause he nodded. “Overwhelming power, an aura like the tide. Suffocating!”

“Yes. Nothing trains a dragon slayer better than experiencing a battlefield and smelling blood. You felt a Dragon King's power: absolute strength that numbers alone cannot oppose. We all have dragon blood; dragons are half our ancestry. Our bloodline makes us instinctively want to submit to them. Only the strongest will and finest blood can preserve dignity before a Dragon King and kill him! So Cassell must train not a crowd, but the elite of the elite, heroes among heroes, incomparable like Meinhard Cassell, the first president of the Lionheart Society.” Anjou looked into Caesar's eyes, his voice low. “Because the worst time... is almost upon us.”
“The worst time?”

“The Dragon Kings on the other three thrones of the Four Monarchs will all awaken. Myth foretold a collective awakening, and Norton's awakening proves the prophecy. You wanted to know when the next Dragon King would wake? Perhaps... today!”
“A collective awakening...?” Caesar drew a deep breath.

“So we can no longer wait. We must choose the finest bloodline among outstanding candidates and devote everything to training that person. He will be the Dragon Kings' mortal enemy.” Anjou paused. “The world's savior.”
“Me?” Caesar pointed at himself.
“Possibly you,” Liza said.

“If devoting everything to my training means more classes and drills, forget it. I'm not good at that. My GPA's only 2.7, as bad as the former president's at Yale, as the principal already said.” Caesar shrugged.
“No. What we intend to strengthen is your bloodline,” Frost said slowly.
“Strengthen my bloodline?”
“Did you know someone can possess more than one Yanling?”
“No.”
“Did you know some hybrids can attain the power of purebloods while remaining hybrids?”
“No.”
“Have you heard of a ‘hybrid monarch’?”
“Comparable to the Four Monarchs?”

“Perhaps even surpassing a Dragon King!” Frost enunciated every word. “That is the Nibelungen Project: strengthen the bloodline, break through the hybrid's limits and the theories in textbooks. Caesar, this is no fantasy. The Secret Party's council of elders can do it. It is a tremendous gift, and we are choosing one person to receive it. Acceptance means power, but also enormous sacrifice. You will face every danger and may even die. Are you willing?”
For once Caesar looked directly at his uncle. Frost's solemn face resembled a preaching pastor's. The room was dead silent; everyone watched Caesar.
Caesar licked his lips. “Why does this feel a little like... wedding vows?”
“Caesar!” Frost was furious.
Anjou laughed aloud.

“Great sacrifice, every danger, risking my life: none of that's much. If giving up those little things would put someone at the top of the hybrids, plenty at the college would accept.” Caesar raised an eyebrow. “I'm only curious why you chose me.”
“Because you're good enough,” Anjou said.
“Why not Chu Zihang?”
“He lacks experience killing a Dragon King directly. In that respect he falls short of you.”
“Why not Lu Mingfei?”
Anjou smiled. “Mingfei's still new. Many people think giving him S-rank was my mistake.”

“But you value him. He shot a Dragon King and gravely wounded the target. When we faced Constantine, you used Yanling: Time Zero and handed him the sniper rifle. Without doubt you expected him to deliver the final shot, though he missed.” Caesar's voice was cold. “You might casually give someone S-rank, but I don't believe you'd entrust your life to a useless nobody while fighting a Dragon King at close quarters.”

“And your uncle insisted you were the best,” Anjou said. “He said ability means not just bloodline, but organization and leadership. We need a leader people will follow as well as a genius. You're a brilliant leader among the new generation; not even Chu Zihang can match you there. Under you the Student Council has grown into a club able to rival the Lionheart Society. So we made you the Nibelungen Project's first candidate.”
Frost had mastered his anger. His low voice was gentle. “Caesar, do you understand now? The family has always loved you selflessly... and placed its hopes in you!”

From Frost Gattuso, this was naked praise and support, a declaration of his determination to put Caesar on a throne. Yet the trustees were silent; no one objected. The candidates had been rigorously selected in advance, and Caesar truly was the best choice. Everyone acknowledged it.
Caesar kept his head down, playing with his fingers as he listened to his uncle finish.
“Uncle, have you ever lost the most important person in your life?” He slowly raised his head and asked the strange question.

“Oh, I forgot. A man like you doesn't have anyone important in his life. So you don't know that people who've experienced that often become particularly stubborn and resistant to certain things. Psychologists say”—Caesar smiled and pointed to his heart—“it's a mental illness.”
“I refuse.” Caesar rose and bowed. “If there's nothing else, excuse me.”

Leaning against an ivy-covered marble column, Caesar leisurely drank an iced gin and watched the luxury cars leave the hotel gates one by one. Last came the mountain bike. Seeing its rider wiggle his rear as he pedaled hard, Caesar couldn't help laughing.
“Is it fun challenging the authority of the family and the trustees?” Frost Gattuso had silently appeared at his side.

“At Cassell I'm only a student. Trustees are exalted people we can't afford to offend. But I said ‘I refuse’ and made them end their meeting without a result, made you important people come for nothing, and made one of you wiggle his rear on the way home. I thought that was amusing,” Caesar said coldly.
“Your childishness is truly intolerable to the family.”

Caesar laughed softly. “You know, Uncle, I guessed why you wanted me when I went in. Though the ‘hybrid monarch’ surprised me, I was right that you meant to promote me. I've been holding it in and playing a game with you, wondering what expression you'd make when I said, ‘I refuse.’”

Frost wasn't angry. He sighed quietly. “What put such a cruel streak in your heart? You're a genius the family rarely sees in centuries, first-rate in blood and talent. You want to be a leader too, and you've always worked hard. The family loves you and wants to help. Chu Zihang and Lu Mingfei may obstruct your path; we don't want that. You're the best; no one should be ranked above you. The family is promoting the Nibelungen Project to secure your future position.”
“My bloodline? Uncle, you've forgotten something. I inherited only half of the Gattusos' noble blood. The other half came from a lowly name, lowly...” Caesar's smile vanished. “Gullveig.”

“Still dwelling on your mother's death?” Frost shook his head. “It seems the misunderstanding between us runs deep. To the family, Gullveig's bloodline was indeed not noble. Her marriage to your father wasn't blessed by the family. But you're different. The entire family recognizes you as its descendant with the finest blood. Your talent has proved it.”

“A lowborn woman marries a husband of noble blood, bears a child, and dies. His family despises her blood but accepts the child mixed with it.” Caesar looked down and laughed. “It's like a story where nobody likes pigs because they're dirty, but when one dies, people cut off the tenderest pork chop. A chef carefully fries it with matsutake and morels, lays it on a spotless china plate, and serves it on a silver tray.”

“Caesar, trust the family. Your mother's death had nothing to do with us. Her funeral was held at Westminster Cathedral, the pope himself presided, and the entire family attended. Her soul is at rest.”
“Don't be ridiculous. We're a family descended from dragons; we don't believe in religion. A funeral conducted by the pope counts as compensation?”

“It was an honor in mourning. The family honored her in return for her contribution.” Frost was deeply earnest. “Caesar, you are her contribution. Think: the only thing she left from her life was you. If her spirit lives, wouldn't she want to see you achieve a man's great work? The Nibelungen Project is the family's love for you, a gift without equal. Refusing it would hurt your mother too. She's watching you from heaven.”
“No. She can't see.” Caesar slowly lifted his head. His expression had changed. Few had seen the face he kept hidden: a cold, thin smile, ice in his eyes.

“When she died, she couldn't see or hear anymore. That was the price she paid to give birth to me.” Caesar looked at his hand. “All I could do then was hold her hand.” He slowly clenched his fist; his knuckles cracked softly. “I didn't dare let go, because I thought how terrible it must be... She couldn't see or hear. If no one held her hand, she'd feel that no one in the world wanted her anymore. She knew nothing of the honors the family gave her. The only connection between her and the world was the warmth passing from my palm.” Caesar laughed hoarsely. “Uncle, I'll repeat what I told you: I'm Gullveig's descendant. I'm not that close to you Gattusos.”
Frost watched him, seeming to see the sorrowful, surging force pouring from his body. After a long time, he sighed again.
“Caesar, look at the sea. The wind's rising. It's going to rain,” Frost said suddenly.
Caesar followed his gaze to the rolling Gulf of Genoa. Dark clouds were gathering, heavy as lead.

“Before you came in, the family had a disagreement with Anjou,” Frost said softly. “We have just killed the King of Bronze and Fire. In the face of such an epoch-making miracle, why argue? Because the waves are rising. A new era is coming.”
“A new era?”

“Hybrids can kill Dragon Kings now. At last we see hope of ending the dragons' history. Afterward, hybrids will be the world's finest people, far superior to ordinary humans. With dragons gone, no one can stand against us. The world's order will be rewritten, as in the Age of Exploration, as in the Industrial Revolution. That will be the age of hybrids, and you will be their leader.” Frost sounded like a poet singing of a glorious future. “The family is putting all its strength behind you now. Isn't that enough proof of our love? You will be the new era's... emperor!”
His voice held a faint temptation, like the serpent in Eden telling Adam and Eve, “Eat the fruit of that tree, and you will stand beside God.”
Caesar turned his glass in his hand and said nothing.

“Think again, Caesar. If you're willing, the family will raise the Nibelungen Project at the next board meeting, with you as the sole candidate. Many people dream of this opportunity. Now the family offers it to you; please accept.” Frost coaxed him patiently. “Don't miss the best moment. Understand that the family cannot absolutely control the board. Sooner or later the project must begin to oppose the Dragon Kings' collective awakening. If you give it up, Chu Zihang or Lu Mingfei will take your place. Opportunity won't wait forever for one person.”
“Yes, I long to prove myself. I long for glory and power.” Caesar lifted his head.
“Good. That's what we hoped to hear.”

“But I'm different from you.” Caesar turned and looked at Frost coldly. “I'll seize my own future with my own hands. Chu Zihang, Lu Mingfei, anyone else who might threaten me—I'll compete with them face to face! One day I'll have everything I want, not as head of the Gattuso family, but as Caesar. Just Caesar, like the man my Dictator was named for. Take back your gift. It's a little dirty.”
A cold sea wind blew between uncle and nephew as they met each other's eyes, neither willing to show weakness.

At last Frost looked away. He sighed. “Hatred takes only an instant to build, but love takes many years. Caesar, you're still too young. One day you'll understand the family's love.” He drew an envelope from his coat, the Gattuso crest stamped in red sealing wax. “I brought a letter from your father. I meant to give it to you at the celebration launching the Nibelungen Project... The family knows whom you love. Regrettably, her blood, like your mother Gullveig's, isn't noble enough. By rights, bloodline is the absolute standard when the family chooses a bride. But we don't want your mother's tragedy repeated, and we're willing to change the rules for you.”

“If you're willing to accept the Nibelungen Project's gift,” Frost said, looking into Caesar's eyes, “the family will make an exception and approve your engagement to Chen Motong. Your union will have the family's blessing.”
Caesar stared. Slowly he finished his drink. “How generous...”

“You should understand how enormous the family's blessing on your engagement is. Do you still doubt us? The family blesses only its future head's marriage. You are that future head. Surely you don't want your future wife Chen Motong denied our blessing? How pitiable she would be!”
With a loud crash, Caesar's glass shattered on the ground, scattering pale pink shards.
“My engagement has nothing to do with the family. Now take your generosity and”—Caesar bit the tip of his tongue and spat one savage word with the force of someone hawking up phlegm—“get lost!”
A startling rage burst from his eyes. They even glimmered faintly gold, a sign that in a hybrid appeared only at extremes of emotion.
His dragon blood boiled fiercely!

In the distance, Anjou also drank gin, watching uncle and nephew with a faintly mischievous smile. Without Kamaitachi's hearing he couldn't make out their words, but their changing expressions were enough to make the drama entertaining.
At last Frost turned away in anger, leaving Caesar alone looking at the sea. His lowered eyes were shadowed, no longer pure ice blue but dark and deep like the sea under cirrus clouds.
“A family melodrama,” Anjou said with a shrug. His phone rang. He answered, then frowned a few seconds later. “Chu Zihang's in trouble again?”
Runde Building, 18:57.

The headlights of the van marked “FedEx” suddenly came on. As their beams pierced the rain, its old engine made a dreadful noise, like an old man drawing a great breath into withered lungs, preparing to drive his stiff, aged muscles at any cost. The van burst through the glass curtain wall in a storm of shards and struck a wedge-shaped load-bearing pillar. The pillar stopped it and split its front end in two, like a sharp blade cutting into an enemy's skull.

Sparks flew from the engine, the radiator burst, and white steam filled the air. The entire building shook, but not as violently as the maintenance men's hearts. The windshield had broken. The cab was empty.

This was the van they had driven here. The key was still in one man's pocket, and they had left nobody inside. Yet while they threw the shopping floors into chaos, the driverless van had been silently circling the building, like a beast circling prey, seeking an opening.
Was this utterly lifeless van... trying to hunt humans?

Supernatural events were hardly unusual to maintenance men with dragon blood, and they immediately escalated their response. One drew a flare gun, knelt, and fired. A dazzling red signal flare shot through the glassless window into the van.

To these men a flare gun could hardly be called a weapon; they had once slaughtered enemies with submachine guns in both hands. This one was an exception. Its enormous recoil knocked a former SEAL who could bench-press 250 pounds flat on his back. The “flare” screamed through the entire vehicle, flew out of the building, and melted a twenty-centimeter hole in an aluminum-alloy sculpture in the center of the square.
“Can that... still be called a flare?” The maintenance man felt as if he had fired a miniature rocket.

But he ought to be used to it: this was the Equipment Department's style, perverse modifications, immense power, and... vague instructions. When the launcher was issued, the armorer had casually insisted that it be fired vertically to avoid “unpredictable” consequences. Now the man understood that it really was sound advice. Firing a rocket at any target would have “unpredictable” consequences.
Still, it had been fired. Surely not even a ghost could withstand a weapon from the Equipment Department? The men exchanged glances.
Everything seemed normal again. The van that had suddenly moved by itself had caused no trouble... Then a piercing metallic scrape reached their ears, like a steel cable... breaking.
Seconds later, a tremendous crash sounded outside the glass wall. The suspended platform, weighing hundreds of kilograms, smashed into the asphalt.
The maintenance men stared in shock. According to the schedule, Chu Zihang... had been on that platform!

Chu Zihang floated in the rain. The instant the platform fell, he had jumped with all his strength, head tilted back toward the sky. The whole sky was reflected in his pupils; from this angle every raindrop seemed to fall from one point at its center, all of them destined for his eyes.
Like a god observing the world from the air, he saw it with extraordinary clarity.

In an instant he underwent a transformation as though reborn. Blood rushed through his veins like a great river thawing from ice; every cell breathed recklessly and with all its strength, like a spring bud. Endless power passed silently along muscle and sinew.
He had used blood amplification.

This technique instantaneously increased bloodline purity through mental means. Before the industrial age it had been the deepest secret of certain families, allowing a hybrid body to gain power close to a pureblood dragon's. But it was also regarded as black magic and subjected to many restrictions. After the persecution of heretics in the dark Middle Ages, the secret ceased to be passed down. Not until the early twentieth century did the Secret Party's rising Lionheart Society rediscover it, quickly surpassing the older generation to establish itself as the new generation's leader.
And Chu Zihang was the current Lionheart Society president.

The records preserved by the society said a lion lay hidden in one's bloodline. If you were willing to untie the ropes binding it, you could gain its strength. And what bound that strength was yourself.
The Lionheart Society's original meaning was “the society that releases the lion's heart.”

With a motion no human could possibly perform, Chu Zihang stepped against the glass curtain wall and used a moment's friction to check his fall. He threw away the scabbard and drove Murasame through the glass. The force of his descent left a smooth cut down its surface!

He exerted force with one hand and leaped back onto the twenty-first floor. Confronted by his sudden return, the guards showed no panic, as though they saw nothing astonishing in defying gravity. They tightened their grips on their batons; some unfastened iron chains from their waists. Chu Zihang looked around, eyes unfocused. He wasn't looking at the eager guards at all; those antlike things did not exist in his sight.

If a god looked down on the world, would he gaze at every passerby? It was like a child crouching beside a tree root, watching ants busily going in and out and poking a stick into their nest, without truly looking at any individual ant.
Once you possessed the power to reduce an individual to ashes with ease, you would no longer notice its existence.

His sunglasses had fallen during the descent. Blazing golden eyes lit the mist. The guards began to retreat; the majesty of those pupils opposed the Yanling controlling them. It was a gaze from on high, as though a hand gripped each heart and would crush it if the owner resisted and failed to answer.

The faint, dreamlike song suddenly rose, piercing the air like a blade, and the domain expanded at once. Bright beads of blood seeped from the guards' skin. Their bodies had been strengthened to the limit; their blood pressure was so high that capillaries burst. The Yanling overcame the authority of the golden eyes, extinguishing their fear. They leaped again, electric batons high overhead, spiderweb filaments of static entwining them. An attack without a blind spot closed in from every direction at once.
Yanling: Sovereign Flame opened its domain.

Enormous heat filled the confined space. In a few hundredths of a second, the temperature approached eighty degrees Celsius. The heat drove the fog away at once. In a spherical space two meters across, centered on Chu Zihang, the air became completely clear; outside the domain the fog remained, the boundary plainly visible. Guards fell on either side of him before a single baton could touch him. The sudden heat gave their bodies no time to react; their temperatures shot above forty degrees and their brains immediately shut down.

Metal clacked in the fog ahead: a gun being chambered. A guard raised an illegal imitation Black Star pistol and aimed at Chu Zihang's head. Chu Zihang's eyelid twitched. Suddenly he was before the guard, gripping his wrist. He squeezed silently, breaking both wrist bones. He threw the unconscious guard aside. His own hand had entirely changed shape: bones protruded, fine iron-blue scales covered its back, and sharp claws sheathed his nails. Several guards swept iron chains low along the floor, trying to break his shins. He didn't evade, allowing the chains to coil around his legs. They pulled in opposite directions to bring him down. Chu Zihang crouched, seized all the chains, and slowly dragged the guards back toward him. Their muscles bulged, their strength now comparable to bulls, yet he pulled those maddened bulls back by sheer force.

The chains suddenly became searing hot. The guards screamed and let go, but the skin of their palms had burned onto the metal. Sovereign Flame heated the chains until they glowed faintly red. Chu Zihang swung them like red snakes across the guards' backs, leaving black marks; faintly came the sound of bones breaking.

Seconds ago the place had been crowded; now everyone lay on the floor. The smell of burning and a faint scent of blood filled the air. Fog was everywhere, a white expanse hiding the end of the corridor.

The King's Attendants domain that had enveloped the guards suddenly collapsed. They awoke as if from a dream, their bodies completely unable to resist their injuries. Some howled; others fainted from the pain.
Dragging the red-hot chains among the wounded, Chu Zihang seemed like a flame demon emerging from an opened hell.
The guards crawled backward in terror. Chu Zihang still held an utterly aggressive stance, but everyone capable of opposing him had fallen. How could he attack further?
To swing those chains again could only mean slaughter!

He walked past them, chains scraping shrilly. His eyes held none of the howling men; he simply advanced down the vapor-filled corridor, still in a fully attacking posture. The guards stared, wondering whether he had gone mad. Ahead was only an empty doorway; nobody remained inside.
With a hiss, a cold curtain of water fell from above. The fire-safety system had begun spraying, alerted by Sovereign Flame's heat.
An empty corridor, bodies covering the floor, thick fog, water falling from the sky... Chu Zihang wiped his face. It felt like standing alone in a rainy night.

He advanced step by step. A red “Exit” sign flashed in the mist at the corridor's end. Thuds came from the door, as though someone were pounding madly to get out; at some point the pounding became deafening. He kicked the door open. Denser white vapor poured out. Under deathly pale fluorescent light stood those strangely familiar shadows whose faces one could never remember, silently greeting him with expressionless faces and whispered murmurs, exactly like the reception six years ago.
The guards couldn't see them, but to him they were exceptionally real. The twenty-first floor was full of people, walking slowly out of the fog toward Chu Zihang, their faces blank.
He removed the earpiece from behind his ear, threw it down, and crushed it underfoot, severing contact with everyone else.
What followed really could only be slaughter. That man had once said there was no need for mercy toward these things, because they could not even be called living people.
“Abort the operation! Withdraw personnel!” Manstein seized the microphone and shouted. “The police are almost here! No one can fall into their hands! Where is Chu Zihang? Where is Chu Zihang?”

On the globe projection, a red dot in East Asia flashed rapidly, alarms sweeping through the central control room. The operation there was sliding out of control. Manstein didn't know what had happened; an elaborately designed operation had been thrown completely off rhythm by a ghostly driverless van. They had lost contact with Chu Zihang, and no one knew what was happening on the twenty-first floor. The terrible cracking before communications failed was chilling.
“Continue the operation.” Schneider suddenly reached over and seized the microphone, stopping him. “I know where Chu Zihang is.”
Schneider brought up a login screen and entered a password. A cross section of the Runde Building appeared, with a rapidly blinking red dot on the twenty-first floor.
“That's Chu Zihang,” Schneider said quietly. “He's all right, moving on the twenty-first floor.”
“Thank goodness.” Guderian held his chest and breathed out deeply.
Manstein stared. “What's he doing?”
“I don't know...” Schneider said.

At that moment in China, eighteen thousand kilometers away, Murasame, trailing flickering firelight, cut through the fog again and again, leaving transparent slashes in the air that crossed like a calligraphy practice sheet written with fierce strokes. Ink-black shadows rushed at him one after another, only to be swept into splashes of thick darkness by the blade, shattering in the mist into countless threads of ink. When black blood coated Murasame's edge, clear drops condensed on it and washed the darkness away. Chu Zihang paused briefly and looked around, holding the sword across his left arm, its point sloping down as ink-dark drops fell slowly from it. More black shapes stepped out of the mist. He had no time to distinguish reality from illusion, just as on that night in the typhoon. Then he had been a frail boy; now he had set his dragon blood alight. Without hesitation, without asking why, he sent a storm of blades cutting through the fog once more.
What were his enemies? He needed only to cut them down!

The ground-floor shopping area had completely changed. Some maintenance men helped guards evacuate frightened crowds; others fought a fire. A shop selling ZIPPO lighters had collapsed in the shaking, and lighter fuel had caught fire. Faced with a stranger disaster, the guards had no time for the American muscle men, who seemed merely a little crazy and out for amusement.
“Who's still on the twenty-first floor?” the Maintenance Department leader demanded in fluent Chinese, rushing up to a guard.
“No one! Everyone's evacuated to the twentieth!” the guard shouted. “We've checked every identity.”

An inexplicable chill ran through the leader. If the twenty-first floor was empty, who was holding Chu Zihang up there? His suddenly quickened breathing before communications failed had given them a bad feeling.
“But he's never disappointed me. He'll bring back what we need.” Schneider checked the clock. “He has more than two minutes. There's still time.”

“Two minutes? According to plan he should already be in the descending elevator with the documents! Still time? The entire operation is out of rhythm! Call your student back!” Manstein was shocked and furious; Schneider's firmness and indifference were completely unexpected. He was violating Executive Department procedures, although the procedures existed to be violated. Manstein couldn't understand his confidence, as though everything were still under control.
“I can't call him back. I can't reach him either. The schedule is broken, so it's broken. He's already left your plan,” Schneider said coldly.
“Left the plan?”
“He's still operating, but not along your planned track. He'll retrieve the documents independently. I told you sending him alone was enough. The team is an obstacle to him, not support.”

“He... alone?” Manstein could hardly believe his ears. This was an SS-rank mission. Norma had repeatedly simulated the plan and excluded risks in advance before settling on a nine-person team. Each person had a duty; together they were nine components of a precisely coordinated machine running at high speed. Now one component had broken away and was trying to perform the entire machine's function independently. More ridiculous still, the man who had made that component firmly believed it could succeed. It was as absurd as a racing tire preparing to run an entire rally in place of the car, while its designer applauded the brave tire!
“It's not hard for him. I only hope he doesn't make too much of a mess.” Schneider handed Manstein a stack of documents he had prepared.
Manstein opened them in confusion. After the first few paragraphs his expression changed; his pupils widened and glimmered faintly gold.
“His previous mission reports. The real versions. The ones you found in Norma were polished by me,” Schneider said mildly.
After half a page Manstein closed the folder. Silent for several seconds, he drew a deep breath. “Schneider... do you know what your student is?”
“No, but he's very useful. He's still an intern, but he's the Executive Department's ace commissioner.”
“But you don't trust him.” Manstein stared into his eyes. “So you planted a transmitter on him. Does he know?”
Schneider looked out the window. “He doesn't. It isn't a question of trust. If you have a sharp knife, you always want to know where it is, so it doesn't accidentally cut someone.”
“Where is the transmitter?”
“He had a tooth filled in the college infirmary. It was implanted in a molar then, covered by a titanium-alloy crown. Even X-rays won't show it.”
“Even someone with that fine a bloodline gets cavities?” Guderian said.

“I was oddly relieved when I learned he did,” Schneider said quietly. “It makes him seem human. Humans are supposed to be a flawed species: they get sick, feel pain, and grow afraid. They aren't perfect, but they're more real.”

“What do we do now? Just wait? Three professors on duty are responsible for an operation, and all we can do is wait more than ten thousand kilometers away for your prized student to turn in a satisfactory answer?” Manstein frowned tightly.
“Ninety-five seconds left. He'll hand it in. He's always punctual,” Schneider said.

“Dad, listen. I have... Do you have paper and a pen? If not, get them! Quickly!” Curled under his desk, Tang Wei clutched the landline. Only this heavy huanghuali-wood furniture could make him feel safe now; with his back against its thick panel, his heart was beating just slowly enough to avoid a heart attack.

“I have three bank cards, Bank of Communications, China Merchants, and ICBC. I wrote the numbers inside the blue photo album at home. The password is your birthday backward... Dad, don't interrupt. Let me finish. I'm busy and have to hang up soon.” Tang Wei panted, fighting to keep his voice from shaking and giving himself away. “The deeds to our properties are at Auntie's. Six apartments and one shop, seven deeds in all, don't count wrong. I bought a three-million trust in your name; it matures in a year and a half. Don't forget your commercial insurance either, another three million... Oh, right, my watches and jade are valuable too, worth two million together. Don't throw them away.” He wiped his face, but tears kept betraying him. “I'm fine, don't worry. Aren't we applying for visas? I'm telling you how much money we have so you can answer the visa officer... I'm really fine! Why don't you believe me? Can you stop fucking arguing with me? You've fussed over me since I was little. Do you have to do it now too...?”
“I have a visitor. I won't be home for dinner tonight.” He hung up and pulled out the phone cord.

The office was dark. Sprinklers sprayed like mad; rain fell outside and inside the entire building, bitterly cold. The air-conditioning had stopped, the power had failed, and the building was paralyzed. Tang Wei was trapped in this office. A private elevator requiring a VIP card had once come directly here, but now it wouldn't respond no matter how often he swiped. This top-floor office was his real one, known only to a few trusted brothers. He had built a safe into the wall for cash, ledgers, and important things, including the paper envelope of documents. When bored in his twenty-first-floor office, he occasionally took the VIP elevator up to play games, so he kept many personal belongings here too.
Now Tang Wei thought he would die in this office.

He had sensed trouble from the moment that fearsome gang of American muscle men entered the shops. Then came the strange site message and someone breaking into the twenty-first floor, where dozens of his men were stationed—a heavily defended position, in military terms. But when he called down only half a minute later, no one answered. Tang Wei wanted to run, but it was too late.

He had always known a hunter's money wasn't easy. As the saying went, “Live by the underworld, and sooner or later you pay.” He had done so many shady things over the years, digging up dozens of ancestral graves alone, that he wouldn't believe in no retribution himself. He wanted to go to Vietnam because perhaps it was far enough away that retribution, having no sense of direction, couldn't find him. He had earned enough and was supposed to retire tonight. Damn it, in a risky trade like this, “retire” was a taboo word. Countless masters died the night before retiring: Qu Yang and Liu Zhengfeng, the two old men who understood one another in The Smiling, Proud Wanderer, or Xu Wenqiang in The Bund, preparing to go to France to recover the girl he had lost...
Now retribution had come in overwhelming force. He had already called the police, hoping they'd hurry over and take him to prison for a good reeducation. At least he wouldn't die there.
He should have known the two and a half million dollars had come too easily. Money that easy burned your hands.

Fortunately he had laundered his earnings again and again and transferred them under various names to his father. If he really died, the old man would suddenly discover he was rich.
