A single old bachelor with tens of millions, perhaps a hundred million—who knew how many scheming women would try to seduce him for the inheritance? The thought saddened Tang Wei. When he was little, his mother had left father and son to go south and make money, never to return. His father was a worker who supported him through school on his small factory wage and night work guarding warehouses. Later he retired early to give Tang Wei his job, continuing to guard warehouses himself. Dad never remarried, though life was hard without a woman. It wasn't that he still loved the vanished mother too deeply; he'd told Tang Wei he liked women with fuller chests... But such women all demanded that Tang Wei be sent to Grandma's to be raised. Dad refused. My son can't be raised that way, he'd said. My son's a hooligan! They can't keep him in line; he has to stay with me!

So no woman would live with Dad. Tang Wei thought he should have tricked one into coming to cook and wash for them first; Tang Wei could have stayed with Grandma for a few months and then come back. Dad was such an idiot, determined to keep him close no matter what.

Because Dad was an idiot, Tang Wei had to be tough. There were only two men in the family; one of them had to be tough, or wouldn't everyone bully them to death? When Tang Wei made his first windfall as a hunter, he withdrew every cent in cash, stacked it before his father, and said, “Hey! How about that? Your son's made something of himself, hasn't he? Spend as much as you like! Take it!” Dad said tearfully, “Son, robbing banks gets you executed! Run, quickly, take all the money. I'll stay and hold off the police.”

The memory brought tears streaming down Tang Wei's face. If only he'd found Dad a companion before he died; then he could go in peace. Unfortunately, none of the women Dad saw regularly met his standards: one had bags under her eyes, another skin too dark. Tang Wei would lose face among his friends with any of them as a stepmother.

After crying for a while, he remembered something. Even if his enemies knew about this office, the VIP elevator was out, cutting off the shortcut. They shouldn't be able to reach him before the police arrived.
He crawled out from under the desk, locked the office door, and shoved the desk against it. Feeling hidden in a relatively safe fortress, he breathed a little easier.
He turned his head, and his heart nearly jumped out of his throat...
A pitch-black figure clung to the enormous floor-to-ceiling window!

It was nearly two hundred meters above the ground. Who could climb a two-hundred-meter skyscraper in minutes? Superman or Spider-Man? Rain hammered the figure outside, spray surrounding him like a faint glow. He seemed to wear a suit of iron-blue scales.

Tang Wei screamed and lunged for the crossbow on the wall. He had brought it from America, supposedly for shooting fish, though it was really a weapon. Its compound bolts could pass through three meters of water and pierce a large fish; in air they could easily penetrate sheet metal. He pulled the string back with all his strength. He no longer cared about human life; the silhouette alone terrified him! He hoped the top floor's sturdy double-reinforced glass would hold the figure for a moment. He needed a few seconds more.

But the glass... began to melt! Dark-red currents appeared around the shadow, along with a transparent boundary that instantly turned the rain to white steam. Where glass met the boundary, it was like wax meeting fire. The shadow entered the office. Everything near him burned silently, dark-red currents snaking along the transparent edge. Firelight revealed his hideous face, bones jutting sharply at his temples and cheeks.

He was a demon burning with black fire! Tang Wei had robbed countless ancestral graves and encountered evil things more than once, but none was so terrifying. Beside this one, they were innocent, gentle little girls compared with a demon god.

At last Tang Wei cocked the bow and fired, opening his eyes as wide as he could. His pupils burned like a lizard's or snake's, or golden gas lamps. This was his greatest secret, the reason he could make a living as a hunter. When he concentrated fully, his pupils changed color. Until now, every uncanny thing had fled before those golden eyes.
The bolt tore through the air like silk being cut. At this distance, such a powerful shot could not possibly be dodged.
The other man didn't dodge. He raised a hand and waved it lightly; the bolt split in two.

He slowly raised his head. Gold ten times brighter than Tang Wei's shot from his pupils, dimming even the firelight. Tang Wei felt immense force thrust his gaze back. He fell to his knees involuntarily, trembling. The other's eyes were gold too, but possessed an overwhelming advantage in power. Tang Wei no longer dared meet them, and understood why some hunters trembled before his own golden eyes. It was like facing a demon god: radiating golden cracks formed intricate patterns in the pupils, seemingly able to rob a person of his mind.

A huge force slammed Tang Wei against the wall, feet off the ground. A hand like an iron clamp gripped his neck, his cervical bones on the verge of cracking. His whole body convulsed, but he had no room to struggle. The clamp tightened slowly; blood failed to reach his brain, his thoughts grew confused, his sight blurred. Though the other seemed surrounded by flame, Tang Wei felt no heat from the hand. Those golden eyes filled his vision, slowly opening and closing. They could never be human eyes: not a trace of mercy. He observed the dying Tang Wei with indifferent curiosity, like a child poking an ant to death with a twig.

His neck bones made a strange cracking sound. Tang Wei had never imagined how terrifying it would be to hear his own neck break. He knew he was really going to die. Now he wished the other would be quick.
Because facing those eyes was more terrifying than death!

The other suddenly released him, letting him fall flat on his face. Tang Wei had barely recovered a little awareness and hadn't decided whether to be relieved when the man turned and picked up a heavy steel fire extinguisher.
“Is he going to smash me to death?” Tang Wei's heart clenched. He couldn't really say whether being strangled or smashed was better, but was it so hard to make it quick?
The other pressed the nozzle and sprayed Tang Wei vigorously, extinguishing the flames on him. Only then did Tang Wei notice that his clothes had somehow caught fire.

The man dropped the extinguisher and slowly backed away, each step leaving a black footprint on the carpet. The black-red currents around him gradually faded, and the hazy boundary vanished. The iron-blue scales on his skin retracted beneath it like insects withdrawing after poking out their heads. He was no demon god or monster, but a handsome young man, scarcely more than a boy. Soaked through in a FedEx uniform, he looked like a delivery boy collecting a package in the rain, except for the deadly blade in his right hand. Tang Wei stared stupidly for a long moment, then clutched his throat and coughed violently.
The boy sat on the couch, hands resting on the long sword, slowly regulating his breathing.
Tang Wei didn't understand what had happened. He stared at the boy, whose eyes were lowered. He had suddenly changed from a monster back into a boy, yet also seemed to have suddenly grown old.
“Is that your father?” He pointed to a photograph on the wall and asked softly. His voice was unexpectedly gentle, even courteous.

It was an old photograph enlarged to thirty-six inches and set in a rosewood frame. Tang Wei wore a black gown and mortarboard, arm around his father in bright sunshine. Dad's wrinkled face seemed ready to burst into flowers. It was Tang Wei's graduation picture. His university wasn't much, but after so many hard years Dad had raised him to graduation and was immensely proud, telling everyone at the factory and buying a suit especially for the ceremony. Tang Wei hadn't cared much about graduating, but Dad had rented academic dress, forced him to put it on, and paid for the picture. Red words on it read: “July 1994. My son Tang Wei graduates from university. From Father.”
“Mm-hm!” Tang Wei nodded hard. “My dad. Looks like me, doesn't he? Big nose.”

He realized the photograph was precisely why he had survived. But his father wasn't some powerful official like Li Gang, only an ordinary worker with few abilities. What power could he possibly have to make this killer hesitate? Could this be his long-lost twin? But were there twins more than ten years apart in age? Dad's illegitimate son? Could Dad have produced such a handsome illegitimate son? Tang Wei examined the boy while little dramas played out in his head.
“You do look alike.” The boy nodded and checked his watch. “No more talk. My time is limited. You took something you shouldn't have.”
Without a word Tang Wei opened the safe, took out the paper envelope, and offered it carefully with both hands.
“You haven't opened it?” The boy glanced at the intact seal.
“No, no. It's the client's property; how would we dare peek? It was supposed to be sent tonight, and then you came.” Tang Wei bowed and scraped.
“Sorry for the financial loss.” Carrying the envelope, the boy walked to the window.
He leaped out and vanished into the vast curtain of rain.

Tang Wei stood stunned for several seconds, then collapsed limply onto the floor. With shaking hands he took out his phone and called Dad. As soon as the call connected, Dad shouted and cursed in alarm and anger: Tang Wei had spouted all that ominous nonsense and hung up, then wouldn't answer when called back. He had frightened Dad nearly into a heart attack.

“What the fuck are you yelling about? The guest has gone. I'm coming home for dinner, so save me something hot.” Tang Wei hung up impatiently. He leaned wearily against the bookcase and began wondering again whether Dad had secretly cheated behind his back.

The grandfather clock boomed, its chimes echoing around the office walls. Tang Wei shuddered, remembering the courier supposed to collect the mail at seven. The courier his employer mentioned was this boy, and in the intended ending he would be dead by now, except for that photograph.
At Cassell headquarters, the central control-room clock changed to 19:00. On the globe projection, the red dot in East Asia vanished at once. Schneider raised his head and slowly exhaled.
“Mission complete,” Manstein said quietly. “Schneider, you were right. He's perfectly capable of doing it alone. He can't work with anyone... His bloodline is too strong.”
“For a student who pursues ‘the strongest,’ only ‘the strongest’ earns a passing grade. Everything else fails.” Schneider showed no relief. “That's also his greatest flaw.”

“I don't want to congratulate you on such a fine student.” Manstein was grave. “He's had another problem. One minute and fifty seconds after the operation began, he completely abandoned our plan. Though he retrieved the documents, we don't know what he did during those three minutes and ten seconds. And the many injuries he caused... Cleaning up won't be easy. I'm worried the bill will be enormous, but you know that's not the greatest trouble...”
Schneider nodded. “The mission report. He may have been on the edge of losing control this time.”
“I can pretend not to know, but you must find a way to deal with it. You know the harm a dangerous bloodline can do us,” Manstein said. “Don't let personal feelings cloud your judgment.”
“Yes. Sometimes I'd rather he were like Lu Mingfei, with no particular ability,” Schneider said softly.
“What nonsense!” Guderian protested. “Mingfei is inspiration from head to toe!”
“Ridiculous. What part did your star pupil play in this operation? He's having dinner with a girl!” Schneider and Manstein said together.
